# **The Database Is the Source of Truth. Your Agent Only Reads the Repo**


[DV Engineering](https://medium.com/@dv-engineering?source=post_page---byline--644b1cff0051---------------------------------------)


6 min read


·


2 hours ago


--


*Written By:* Matthew Weiss


In AI-aided development, even with a well-defined agents.md file and a detailed prompt, your agent can still make a fatal assumption: it sees a relationship in your ORM files and assumes a foreign key constraint enforces it, then builds accordingly when no such constraint actually exists in the database. That wrong assumption becomes the foundation for the next 15 minutes of its work, wasting your time and your token budget.


Why does this keep happening as the models get smarter? Because your agent only reads the repo, and the repo is only a piece of the puzzle; the database contains the other missing pieces. Some of that context never appears in the code at all: DB-side validations and triggers won’t show up in your ORM, and the test data developers rely on is inaccessible to agents. A developer missing that information would ask for it or check first; an agent starts guessing.


The fix is about 15 minutes of setup. Give your agent read-only access to the database itself, and it stops guessing and starts knowing, testing its own queries against real data and even end-to-end testing the feature it just wrote.


## Giving Your Agent Its Missing Context


By the end of this section, you’ll have:


- An MCP server that your agent can query directly
- Credentials that prevent your agents from wreaking havoc in your data layer
- A generated schema that agents without this MCP can use to get started in your codebase, write away.


### MCP Installation


To keep this article sharp, I’ll focus on Postgres and MongoDB as database technologies, since this covers both NoSQL and SQL examples and aligns with the tech stack I use on my team. With the targets chosen, the first move is to get the agents wired in. This is a prerequisite for giving your agents crucial DB context.


### Make Writes Impossible


For credentials, I’ve configured both the MCP tool itself and the credentials I provided to be read-only. Remember that even though you may instruct your agent to “never write to the database”, these are not hard rules, and the agent can simply ignore them, since prompt instructions are guidance, not enforcement.


To ensure data integrity, we need to make it impossible for DB write commands to go through, even if they attempt to. Additionally, queries run through the MCP may be heavy, and data still gets processed by the agent, so I’d stick to your non-production environments for performance and data governance reasons.


With the guardrails in place, the question is whether your agent can actually see the MCPs yet. In Claude, you can verify this with /mcp to see which are listed. If you can’t see them, restarting your instance of Claude or Cursor will usually pick them up.


Now the agent can *check* the schema rather than infer it from your ORM.


### Give the Agent Durable Memory


At this point, you should have a working MCP and be ready to let your agent start writing queries. The downside to this is that, just like an agent onboarding to a repo without an agents.md file, every new instance will treat your codebase as if it’s seeing it for the first time.


Nothing persists between sessions aside from your agents.md, so it’ll need to learn your database each time. We can speed up subsequent sessions by storing durable knowledge for the agent that can be read into context without a ton of prodding around in the database MCP *every* session.


Let’s have our agent do this work for us this session. The tokens and time we spend now will save us both in the future when working in this repo. The only caveat is that these files will need to be updated whenever there is a significant change in data or architecture, or they risk becoming stale. You can regenerate them with the same prompt or make adjustments that match your setup.


For our first-time setup, this is the prompt I would use for Mongo:


> “Using the \`<MCP name>\` MCP , generate \`docs/mongodb-<schemaName>-reference.md\` so
>
>
> future work needn’t re-introspect the DB. Note the env + date.
>
>
> For each collection in the <DB Name> DB find via:
>
>
> schema, indexes, count, and 1–2 sample docs. Per collection, document its purpose, a field table, indexes (flag unindexed fields), 2–3 copy-pasteable example queries, and gotchas.
>
>
> Add an overview table and Mermaid ER diagram up front. Document only what you observe. Mention this file in your agents.md and claude.md”


This is the prompt I would use for Postgres:


> “With read-only access to the Postgres DB (<table or database here>), generate \`docs/postgres-reference.md\` so future work needn’t re-introspect it. Note the env + date.
>
>
> For each table (enumerated via \`information_schema\`): columns + types, primary/foreign keys, indexes, row count, and 1–2 sample rows. Per table, document its purpose, a column table, indexes + FKs (flag unindexed filter columns), 2–3 copy-pasteable example queries, and gotchas. Add an overview table and Mermaid ER diagram up front. Document only what you observe.
>
>
> Mention this file in your agents.md and claude.md files.”


The resulting artifacts of this are a Markdown file and a reference to it in your claude.md. The complexity of this can be quite large and uses a fair amount of context. Since it’s not being added directly to your claude.md, it should only be referenced when needed. You can share this with other developers on your team to get immediate benefits even without them setting up their MCPs.


Every future session starts with verified facts about your database, not assumptions reconstructed from code.


## From Guessing to Knowing


Agents are aware of what’s in the database, which changes how you can test. Unit tests with fixtures still have their place, since they run in CI, independent of any database. But fixtures drift when they aren’t maintained, and with DB access, an agent can validate them against real data and update them when they’ve fallen out of sync. It can also go a step further and end-to-end test the endpoint it just changed. Instead of you hunting down the right test data, the agent already knows what exists and can use it directly. The setup and maintenance steps you’d normally do yourself just disappear.


That’s testing against data. The bigger win shows up while you’re still writing the code. Database access lets agents test the queries they write. For complicated query languages like MongoDB’s, that’s a tremendous timesaver, since untested aggregation pipelines are error-prone for agents and humans alike. The same goes for implementing APIs: rather than manually checking that data persisted correctly, you can defer to the agent and let it self-correct. It saves the back-and-forth and gives your agents the tools they need to validate their own work.


Additionally, it allows for conversational data access. You can ask “How many of x entity, of type y, exist with z parameters?” This may require information across multiple collections and deep knowledge of the relationships between the data.


Rather than banging your head against the wall trying to write this one-off lookup, you can now defer to AI, freeing up your time for other tasks. While I only connect to our development environment or locally, the query it generates is usable in other environments when debugging something in a higher-level environment. So its benefits are not limited to local development work.


## The Payoff


Your database is as fundamental to your projects as the code in your repository, so you can’t expect your agents to perform well without this crucial missing context. Spend these 15 minutes once in this session, and you’ve turned that blind spot into something every future session can read on its own.
